title: Model Diagnostics and Comparison
text: use three-variable causal chain running example throughout.
code: library(because)  set.seed(42) N <- 150  Temperature <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)    # Exogenous NDVI        <- 0.6 * Temperature + rnorm(N, 0, 0.8)   # Mediator Abundance   <- 0.4 * NDVI + 0.3 * Temperature + rnorm(N, 0, 1)  sim_data <- data.frame(Temperature, NDVI, Abundance) # Causal model: Temperature -> NDVI -> Abundance, Temperature -> Abundance fit <- because(   equations = list(     NDVI      ~ Temperature,     Abundance ~ NDVI + Temperature   ),   data    = sim_data,   dsep    = TRUE,   WAIC    = TRUE,   # Required for model comparison   n.iter  = 12500,   n.burnin = 2500 )  summary(fit)

title: Model Diagnostics and Comparison
text: summary() output includes Rhat (Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic; Gelman & Rubin, 1992) n.eff (effective sample size) parameter. Rhat < 1.05: Good convergence; parameter estimates reliable. Rhat 1.05–1.1: Borderline. Consider running iterations thinning aggressively interpreting results. Rhat > 1.1: Non-convergence. chains mixed. interpret estimates. Note modern thresholds: Vehtari et al. (2021) showed classical Rhat < 1.1 criterion can miss non-convergence heavy-tailed posteriors recommend Rhat < 1.01 high-quality inference. adopt Rhat < 1.05 practical intermediate target; aim < 1.01 possible. n.eff > 400: Recommended reliable 95% credible interval bounds (tail quantiles). Values n.eff > 100 sufficient posterior means medians, tail estimates sensitive low effective sample sizes. n.eff < 100: Estimates may unstable. Increase n.iter n.thin.
code: # The stored summary object has $statistics containing Rhat and n.eff sum_stats <- fit$summary$statistics  # Identify parameters with potential convergence issues if (!is.null(sum_stats) && "Rhat" %in% colnames(sum_stats)) {   high_rhat <- sum_stats[sum_stats[, "Rhat"] > 1.05, , drop = FALSE]   if (nrow(high_rhat) == 0) {     cat("All parameters converged (Rhat < 1.05).\n")   } else {     print(high_rhat)   } } else {   # summary() prints results to console; inspect Rhat column visually   summary(fit) }

title: Mediation Analysis
text: Causal inference often requires investigating effect occurs. X affect Y directly, work mediator M? package provides fully automated Bayesian mediation analysis tool, because_mediation(), decomposes Total Effect exposure outcome : 1. Direct Effect: effect X \Y mediated variables graph. 2. Indirect Effect(s): effect propagated intermediate variables (X \M \Y). calculated multiplying posterior distributions coefficients along path, preserving full uncertainty quantification.

title: Mediation Analysis
text: example, investigate Elevation affects Plant Abundance. hypothesize Elevation acts causal chain involving Temperature Soil Moisture: Elevation determines Temperature (higher elevation \lower temperature). Temperature influences Soil Moisture (lower temperature \lower evaporation \higher moisture). Abundance driven Moisture, Temperature, potentially direct effect Elevation (e.g., due UV radiation partial pressure gases).

title: Mediation Analysis
text: simulate N=200 plots along elevation gradient.
code: library(because)  set.seed(42) N <- 200  # 1. Elevation (Exogenous variable) # Ranges roughly from 500m to 1500m Elevation <- rnorm(N, mean = 1000, sd = 200)  # 2. Temperature (Mediator 1) # Decreases with Elevation (Lapse rate approx effect) # Coef: -0.01 implies 100m climb -> -1 degree C Temp <- 25 - 0.01 * Elevation + rnorm(N, sd = 2)  # 3. Moisture (Mediator 2) # Driven by Temperature. Cooler -> Moister. # We model a negative relationship with Temp. Moisture <- 20 - 2 * Temp + rnorm(N, sd = 5)  # 4. Plant Abundance (Outcome) # - Positive effect of Moisture (+0.5) # - Positive effect of Temperature (+1.5) # - Direct negative effect of Elevation (-0.005) due to harsh conditions Abundance <- 10 + 0.5 * Moisture + 1.5 * Temp - 0.005 * Elevation + rnorm(N, sd = 10)  eco_data <- data.frame(Elevation, Temp, Moisture, Abundance) head(eco_data)

title: Non-Gaussian Distribution Families
text: Use case: Count data variance greatly exceeds mean (e.g., parasite loads, number plant seeds, abundance data). Poisson model assumes \text{Var}(Y) = E(Y). Ecological count data often show overdispersion (\text{Var}(Y) > E(Y)), can inflate Type error Poisson models. Negative Binomial adds dispersion parameter r (estimated data) accommodate extra variance. Negative Binomial model substantially lower WAIC data overdispersed. r_Parasite_Load parameter summary captures estimated overdispersion.
code: set.seed(123) N <- 150  Resource <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)  # Overdispersed counts: large variance relative to mean # MASS::rnegbin: mu = exp(0.8 + 0.6*X), size = 2 (small = more overdispersed) library(MASS) Parasite_Load <- rnegbin(N, mu = exp(0.8 + 0.6 * Resource), theta = 2)  nb_data <- data.frame(   Parasite_Load = Parasite_Load,   Resource = Resource ) # Compare Poisson vs. Negative Binomial fit_pois <- because(   equations = list(Parasite_Load ~ Resource),   data = nb_data,   family = c(Parasite_Load = "poisson"),   WAIC = TRUE,   quiet = TRUE )  fit_nb <- because(   equations = list(Parasite_Load ~ Resource),   data = nb_data,   family = c(Parasite_Load = "negbinomial"),   WAIC = TRUE,   quiet = TRUE )  # Compare WAIC (lower = better fit) because_compare(fit_pois, fit_nb)

what: Example 4: Zero-Inflated Models — ZIP and ZINB
title: Non-Gaussian Distribution Families
text: Use case: Count data zeros expected standard Poisson Negative Binomial distribution. Common ecological surveys (many sites detections, plus genuine count variation occupied sites). Zero-Inflated Poisson (ZIP) models data mixture structural zeros Poisson process. ZINB adds Negative Binomial overdispersion.
code: set.seed(99) N <- 200  Habitat <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)  # ZIP: with probability psi, the count is zero (structural zero); # otherwise it follows a Poisson distribution. psi <- 0.4  # 40% structural zeros lambda <- exp(0.5 + 0.7 * Habitat)  structural_zero <- rbinom(N, 1, psi) Abundance <- ifelse(structural_zero == 1, 0, rpois(N, lambda))  zip_data <- data.frame(   Abundance = Abundance,   Habitat = Habitat ) fit_zip <- because(   equations = list(Abundance ~ Habitat),   data = zip_data,   family = c(Abundance = "zip") )  summary(fit_zip) # psi_Abundance: estimated zero-inflation probability # beta_Abundance_Habitat: effect on the Poisson component (log scale) # Use ZINB when counts are also overdispersed fit_zinb <- because(   equations = list(Abundance ~ Habitat),   data = zip_data,   family = c(Abundance = "zinb") )  summary(fit_zinb)

title: Non-Gaussian Distribution Families
text: Use case: Behaviour scores, habitat quality rankings, dominance rank, pain scales, Likert-scale data. Ordinal models estimate set cutpoints (thresholds) divide latent continuous scale categories. proportional odds assumption means single slope parameter describes effect adjacent-category boundaries.
code: set.seed(7) N <- 200  # Predictor: years of experience Dominance_Rank <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)  # Underlying latent variable latent <- 0 + 1.5 * Dominance_Rank + rnorm(N, 0, 1)  # 4 behaviour categories: Subordinate (1), Low (2), Medium (3), Dominant (4) Behaviour <- cut(latent,   breaks = c(-Inf, -1, 0, 1, Inf),   labels = FALSE )  ord_data <- data.frame(   Behaviour = Behaviour,   Dominance_Rank = Dominance_Rank ) fit_ord <- because(   equations = list(Behaviour ~ Dominance_Rank),   data = ord_data,   family = c(Behaviour = "ordinal") )  summary(fit_ord) # cutpoint_Behaviour[k]: thresholds on the latent scale separating categories k and k+1 # beta_Behaviour_Dominance_Rank: effect on the latent scale (positive = higher categories)

title: Deterministic Nodes: Interactions, tresholds and mathematical transformations
text: can model “tipping points” categorical definitions. example, marmot (Marmota marmota) “Mature” older 2 years.
code: # Predictors Age <- runif(N, 0, 10)  # Deterministic threshold: 1 if Age > 2, else 0 IsMature <- as.numeric(Age > 2)  # Outcome: Mating success depends on Maturity Mating <- 2 * IsMature + rnorm(N, sd = 0.5)  data_logic <- data.frame(Mating = Mating, Age = Age)  # Use I() to wrap the logic fit_logic <- because(     equations = list(         Mating ~ I(Age > 2)     ),     data = data_logic,     n.iter = 1000,     quiet = TRUE )  # The model recovers the effect of the threshold # Parameter: "beta_Mating_Age_gt_2" where "gt" means "greater than" summary(fit_logic)

what: Example 1: Comparing Default and Custom Priors
title: Custom Priors and Mechanistic Constraints
text: example, let’s simulate Absolute Growth Rate grams per day (g/day) hypothetical juvenile birds responding ambient temperature.
code: library(because)  set.seed(42) N <- 30 # Ambient temperature in Celsius (Mean 20C) Temp_Raw <- rnorm(N, mean = 20, sd = 5)  # Center it so '0' represents the mean (20C). # This ensures the intercept represents growth at average conditions, # rather than at 0°C (where the bird would be frozen solid!). Temp_Centered <- Temp_Raw - 20  # True relationship: # Baseline growth at mean temp is 10 g/day. # Every degree of warming above mean adds 0.5 g/day. Growth_g_day <- 0.5 * Temp_Centered + 10 + rnorm(N, sd = 2)  df <- data.frame(Temp_Centered, Growth_g_day)

title: Custom Priors and Mechanistic Constraints
text: many biological contexts, negative effect just unlikely, physically impossible. example, consider relationship Body Mass Metabolic Rate (Kleiber’s Law; Kleiber, 1932). larger animal simply consume less energy smaller one (negative slope), else equal. physics life requires costs scale positively mass (West et al., 1997). However, sample size small measurement error huge, might accidentally estimate negative slope. can prevent enforcing positive prior.
code: # Simulate data following Kleiber's Law: MR = a * Mass^0.75 # Taking logs: log(MR) = log(a) + 0.75 * log(Mass) set.seed(42) Mass <- runif(30, 10, 100) # True scaling exponent is 0.75 # We add enough noise that the estimated slope might be negative by chance Log_Mass <- log(Mass) Log_MR <- 1.5 + 0.75 * Log_Mass + rnorm(30, sd = 2.5)  df_kleiber <- data.frame(Log_Mass, Log_MR)  # Prior: The scaling exponent (slope) must be positive # Physics dictates that metabolic cost increases with mass. positive_prior <- list(     beta_Log_MR_Log_Mass = "dnorm(0, 1) T(0, )" )  # 1. Fit Default Model (Unconstrained) - Log-Log regression fit_default_kleiber <- because(     equations = list(Log_MR ~ Log_Mass),     data = df_kleiber )  # 2. Fit Mechanistic Model (Constrained) fit_mech_kleiber <- because(     equations = list(Log_MR ~ Log_Mass),     data = df_kleiber,     priors = positive_prior )  # Compare Estimates summary(fit_default_kleiber) summary(fit_mech_kleiber)  # Visualize: Unconstrained vs. Truncated plot_posterior(     list(Unconstrained = fit_default_kleiber, Mechanistic = fit_mech_kleiber),     parameter = "beta_Log_MR_Log_Mass",     density_args = list(Mechanistic = list(from = 0)) )

what: Example 2: Beta Family for Proportions in (0, 1)
title: Creating Custom Distribution Families
text: Continuous proportions — percentage vegetation cover, task completion rates, dietary proportions — bounded 0 1. Gaussian model can predict values outside range; Beta distribution natural choice. Beta distribution parameterised mean \mu \(0,1) precision (concentration) parameter \phi > 0: Y \sim \text{Beta}(\mu \phi, (1-\mu)\phi) parameterisation, variance \mu(1-\mu)/(\phi + 1): larger \phi means less variance around \mu.
code: beta_prop <- because_family(   name = "beta_prop",    # JAGS: dbeta(shape1, shape2)   # shape1 = mu * phi, shape2 = (1 - mu) * phi   jags_likelihood = paste0(     "{response}[{i}] ~ dbeta(",     "{mu}[{i}] * phi_{response}, ",     "(1 - {mu}[{i}]) * phi_{response})"   ),    link = "logit",   # Logit link maps (-Inf, Inf) to (0, 1)    # Prior on the precision (concentration) parameter   extra_priors = c("phi_{response} ~ dgamma(1, 0.1)"),    description = "Beta distribution for proportions in (0, 1) with logit link" ) set.seed(7) N <- 100  # Predictor: grazing intensity (standardised) Grazing <- rnorm(N, 0, 1)  # Response: vegetation cover proportion in (0, 1) # True relationship on the logit scale logit_mu <- -0.5 - 0.8 * Grazing mu_true  <- 1 / (1 + exp(-logit_mu)) Cover    <- rbeta(N, shape1 = mu_true * 5, shape2 = (1 - mu_true) * 5)  prop_data <- data.frame(Cover = Cover, Grazing = Grazing)  fit_beta <- because(   equations = list(Cover ~ Grazing),   data      = prop_data,   family    = c(Cover = beta_prop()),   n.iter    = 15000,   n.burnin  = 3000 )  summary(fit_beta) # beta_Cover_Grazing: effect on the logit scale (negative = grazing reduces cover) # phi_Cover: estimated precision (higher = lower variance around predicted mean) # Convert from logit scale to probability scale using marginal effects me_beta <- marginal_effects(fit_beta) print(me_beta) # Effect: expected change in Cover (proportion units) per 1-unit increase in Grazing

title: Counterfactual Simulations with the do() Operator
text: Let’s set classic ecological cascade: Temperature drives availability Resource, turn determines Abundance species. also include direct physiological effect Temperature Abundance. define equations fit structural model:
code: set.seed(42) N <- 100  # True parameters # Temperature (mean = 20C, sd = 4C) raw_Temp <- rnorm(N, mean = 20, sd = 4)  # We scale variables for model fitting (Standard practice) df <- data.frame(Site = 1:N) df$Temp <- scale(raw_Temp)   # Resource is driven by Temperature df$Resource <- 0.6 * df$Temp + rnorm(N, 0, 1)  # Abundance is driven by both (Poisson distributed) log_lambda <- 1.2 * df$Resource - 0.5 * df$Temp df$Abundance <- rpois(N, lambda = exp(log_lambda)) eqs <- list(   Resource ~ Temp,   Abundance ~ Resource + Temp )  # Fit the model using JAGS (short chains for vignette speed) fit <- because(eqs, data = df,                 family = list(Abundance = "poisson"),                n.iter = 500, n.burnin = 100, n.chains = 2,                 quiet = TRUE)

title: Bayesian Regression and SEM Diagnostics
text: classical frequentist regression Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), assumption checking dominated null hypothesis significance tests (p-values) Shapiro-Wilk normality, Breusch-Pagan homoscedasticity, rule--thumb Variance Inflation Factors (\text{VIF} > 5). , diagnostics adhere strictly purely Bayesian data analysis philosophy (Gelman et al., 2013; McElreath, 2020). Rather testing sharp null hypotheses models “perfect,” Bayesian diagnostics focus : Posterior parameter covariance geometry: shape joint posterior p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid y) reflect shared information, collinearity, uncertainty trade-offs? (Leamer, 1973, 1978). Posterior predictive checks (PPC): replicated data generated posterior, y^{\text{rep}} \sim p(y^{\text{rep}} \mid y), resemble observed data y across key features quantiles, skewness, variance dispersion? (Gelman, Meng, & Stern, 1996). Randomized quantile residuals: Mapping observations model’s posterior predictive cumulative distribution obtain exact standard normal residuals regardless whether likelihood continuous discrete (Dunn & Smyth, 1996; Hartig, 2022). vignette demonstrates complete diagnostic suite using simulated ecological dataset featuring allometric scaling, collinear predictors, non-linear causal dependencies.

title: Bayesian Regression and SEM Diagnostics
text: Consider ecological study examining drivers animal Migration Tendency. Body Mass (Mass) upstream physiological trait. Brain Size (Brain) scales allometrically Mass, also contains residual variation representing relative encephalization. scale together, Mass Brain exhibit strong collinearity (r \approx 0.90). Precipitation (Precip) environmental driver. Migration Tendency (Migration) causally influenced Mass, Brain (encephalization), Precip. Clutch Size (Clutch) downstream Mass Migration.
code: library(because) library(ggplot2)  set.seed(42) N <- 200  # 1. Exogenous environmental and physiological variables Precip <- rnorm(N, mean = 50, sd = 10) Mass   <- rnorm(N, mean = 3.5, sd = 0.8) # e.g. log body mass  # 2. Allometric brain scaling (log brain mass) # Brain scales with Mass, plus an unmeasured encephalization deviation Encephalization <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 0.25) Brain <- 0.85 + 0.72 * Mass + Encephalization  # Correlation between Mass and Brain is high (~0.90) cor(Mass, Brain)  # 3. Migration tendency (influenced by allometry, encephalization, and climate) Migration <- 1.2 + 0.45 * Brain - 0.20 * Mass + 0.03 * Precip + rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 0.4)  # 4. Downstream clutch size Clutch <- 4.0 - 0.35 * Mass + 0.50 * Migration + rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)  bird_data <- data.frame(Mass, Brain, Precip, Migration, Clutch) head(bird_data)

text: evaluating models fitted across multiple structures, standard across-chain \hat{R} can misleading: chains sampling different candidate structures backbones naturally diverge underlying structures imply different parameter values. check_multicov() resolves computing: 1. \hat{R}_{\text{MCMC}} (Within-Structure Convergence): Convergence within individual structure across replicate chains (\max_k \hat{R}_k). Values < 1.05 indicate reliable MCMC mixing within candidate structure. 2. \hat{R}_{\text{within\_group}} (Within-Group Sensitivity): Parameter sensitivity across candidate structures within group, hypothesis, backbone pseudo-posterior. 3. \hat{R}_{\text{\_group}} (-Group Divergence): Parameter divergence competing hypotheses backbones using Gelman-Rubin ANOVA decomposition. 4. Law Total Variance Decomposition (% Uncertainty): Orthogonally partitions total posterior variance \text{Var}_{\text{total}}(\theta) additive components sum 100\%: - Pct_MCMC: Data estimation / MCMC sampling uncertainty conditional structure. - Pct_Struct: Branch-length / dating / local topological variation within group. - Pct_Group: Structural conflict competing hypotheses/backbones. diagnostic report classifies parameter one four states: - "Invariant": Robust across structures groups (\hat{R}_{\text{MCMC}} < 1.05, \hat{R}_{\text{group}} < 1.05). - "Structure-Sensitive (within group)": Modest sensitivity within-group variation (e.g. tree dating noise), robust across broad backbones. - "Group-Sensitive": Parameter estimates diverge competing hypotheses backbones. - "Check MCMC": Poor within-structure MCMC mixing requiring longer iterations. plotted, check_multicov() displays side--side 2-panel figure: - Left Panel: Forest plot Gelman-Rubin \hat{R} classical 1.05 threshold line. - Right Panel: 100% stacked horizontal bar plot displaying exact uncertainty variance decomposition parameter, aligned row--row left panel.

title: Plot Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE) — plot_rope
text: Region Practical Equivalence (ROPE) formalizes Bayesian equivalence testing (Kruschke 2018; Makowski et al. 2019). evaluating causal paths conditional independence claims d-separation, failure reject sharp null (\(\beta = 0\)) provide evidence absence. ROPE defines explicit negligible boundary \([-\delta, +\delta]\) around zero: Gaussian: default interval c(-0.10, 0.10), representing half Cohen's negligible effect size benchmark (\(\pm 0.1 \times \text{SD}\)) standardized continuous traits (Kruschke 2018). Poisson & Negative Binomial: Coefficients sit log-rate scale (\(\log \text{IRR}\)). default interval c(-0.05, 0.05) represents approximate \(\pm 5\%\) relative change expected count (\(\text{IRR} \[\exp(-0.05), \exp(0.05)] \approx [0.95, 1.05]\)). Binomial, Ordinal, & Multinomial: logistic models, binary outcome modeled via underlying continuous latent variable standard logistic error variance \(\sigma^2 = \pi^2 / 3\) standard deviation \(\sigma = \pi / \sqrt{3} \approx 1.814\). Applying Kruschke's \(0.1 \times \sigma\) rule latent scale yields \(\pm 0.1 \times (\pi / \sqrt{3}) \approx \pm 0.181\) (Gelman et al. 2008; Makowski et al. 2019). corresponds Odds Ratio window \(\text{} \[\exp(-0.181), \exp(0.181)] \approx [0.83, 1.20]\).
